what_its_for: Voriconazole injection is an antifungal medicine used to treat serious fungal infections in your body. It works by stopping the growth of certain fungi that can cause infections in your blood, lungs, throat, or other parts of your body. It is often used when other antifungal medicines have not worked or cannot be used.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you as a slow drip (infusion) into your vein (IV) by a nurse or healthcare provider. You will NOT give this injection to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes about 1 to 2 hours. Do not rush or speed up the infusion on your own. Your healthcare team will prepare the medicine and monitor you during the infusion.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight, the type of infection you have, and how well your kidneys are working. A typical starting dose for adults is 6 mg per kilogram of body weight given twice in the first 24 hours (called a loading dose), followed by a maintenance dose of 4 mg per kilogram every 12 hours. Children may receive different doses. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given in a hospital or clinic setting by a healthcare provider, it is very unlikely you will miss a dose on your own. If you miss an appointment or a scheduled infusion, call your doctor or treatment center right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine yourself — your healthcare team will handle storage. For reference: the unmixed powder is stored at room temperature (59°F to 86°F or 15°C to 30°C). Once the medicine is mixed (reconstituted), it must be used within 24 hours if kept in a refrigerator (36°F to 46°F or 2°C to 8°C). The mixed medicine should never be frozen.
what_to_avoid: While taking voriconazole, avoid direct sunlight and tanning beds because this medicine can make your skin very sensitive to the sun and increase your risk of sunburn or serious skin reactions. Use sunscreen, protective clothing, and sunglasses when outdoors. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it may increase side effects. Do not take many other medicines without first talking to your doctor or pharmacist, because voriconazole interacts with a large number of medications including rifampin, St. John's Wort, certain heart medicines, blood thinners (like warfarin), and many others. Tell ALL of your doctors and pharmacists that you are receiving this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat or pounding in your chest; sudden vision changes, blurred vision, or seeing things that are not there (hallucinations); severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine or pale stools; severe stomach pain; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of your face or throat, or difficulty breathing; confusion or unusual changes in behavior; feeling faint or lightheaded; or unusual bruising or bleeding.
when_it_works: Voriconazole starts fighting the fungal infection right away after your first infusion, but it may take several days before you begin to feel better. Most people start noticing improvement within a few days to a week. It is very important to complete the entire course of treatment your doctor prescribes, even if you feel better, to make sure the infection is fully gone.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Effective birth control must be used during treatment. BREASTFEEDING: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. CHILDREN: This medicine can be used in children 2 years of age and older, but doses are calculated differently. KIDNEY PROBLEMS: If you have kidney problems, your doctor may switch you to the oral (pill) form of voriconazole instead of the injection, because the IV form contains an ingredient that can build up in people with poor kidney function. LIVER PROBLEMS: Your doctor will monitor your liver closely and may adjust your dose if you have liver disease. ELDERLY: No specific dose adjustment is usually needed, but your doctor will monitor you closely.
